description:
FILED s473t6d (Opus, 2026-09-20) by #1501 round 11 (CHECK 2 on t/op/eval.t:360-392).

perl: a sub whose package is `DB` is the debugger's own frame, and a string
eval inside it searches the pad of the sub that CALLED it, not its own.  It is
how `perl -d` evaluates an expression "in the debugged program's scope", and
`t/op/eval.t` asserts it five ways.

REPRODUCER (perl 5.40.3 vs PCL):

    package DB;    sub db3 { eval '$x' }
    package DB;    sub db5 { my $x = 4; eval '$x' }
    package main;  sub db1 { eval '$x' }
    { my $x = 3;
      print db1(), " ", DB::db3(), " ", DB::db5(), "\n";
    }
    perl: 2 3 3      (db1 is NOT a DB sub, so it sees the file lexical 2;
                      db3 and db5 see the CALLER's 3 -- db5's own `my $x=4`
                      does not win)
    PCL:  2 2 4      (each sub sees its own)

ROWS: baselines/perl-suite-fails.tsv op/eval.t 94, 95, 96, 98, 99 (the last
two are the [GH #19370] lexical-sub and anon-sub call sites).

SHAPE: the eval capture alist is built at the CALL SITE's lowering.  A sub in
package `DB` would need the alist of its CALLER instead -- which is a run-time
fact, not a compile-time one, so this is the caller-frame lexical access
`caller()` fidelity (#233) asks for from the other side.  Measure how much of
that machinery exists before designing; five rows is not worth a new frame
model on its own.
subject: an `eval STRING` inside a sub of package DB sees the CALLER's pad (perl's debugger rule); PCL reads its own lexicals
